analysis.one_liner: Creates a dedicated OSHA construction safety office and requires written safety plans on every construction project.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or even a single cosponsor and died in committee when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Occupational Safety and Health Act to add construction-specific rules. It would have created an Office of Construction Safety, Health, and Education inside OSHA, required every construction project to designate a 'project constructor' responsible for a written site safety plan, given workers a way to trigger inspections when imminent danger exists, and required state safety plans to be at least as tough as the federal ones. It also directed the Labor Department to recommend making contractors' safety records a factor in awarding federal construction contracts. The bill was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction workers, who face some of the highest fatality rates of any industry, would gain enforceable site-level safety plans, regular worksite inspections, a toll-free complaint line, and a way to stop work in the face of imminent danger. Responsible contractors who already invest in safety would also benefit from competing against unsafe operators whose poor records would have to be considered in federal contract awards.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every construction project to have a written safety and health plan, developed by a designated 'project constructor,' including hazard analysis, regular worksite inspections, and a competent person on site at all times [S3].
Gives any construction employer, employee, or employee representative a mechanism to request an inspection when imminent danger exists and to stop work or remove workers from the dangerous area [S3].

Creates an OSHA Office of Construction Safety, Health, and Education that would identify employers with high fatality or injury rates or a pattern of noncompliance, and establishes a toll-free line for complaints and reports [S2, S3].
Requires state safety plans covering construction to be at least as effective as the federal requirements, preventing states from maintaining weaker rules [S2, S3].

Directs the Labor Secretary to recommend legislative changes that would make bidders' safety records a criterion in awarding federal construction contracts, rewarding safe contractors over repeat violators [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Construction owners and general contractors, who would bear the cost of designating project constructors, developing and administering written safety plans, and taking on liability — the bill makes project constructors count as 'employers' for citation and penalty purposes. Contractors with poor safety records would also risk losing federal work once safety records became an award criterion.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden would fall on construction owners and contractors, who would have to designate a project constructor, produce and maintain a written plan for every project, and accept citation liability for that role — costs that on small projects could be significant relative to the work [S3].

Making the project constructor an 'employer' for citation purposes raises liability questions for owners who do not directly control the work of every subcontractor on site, a concern construction industry groups typically raise with mandated multi-employer responsibility [S3].

The bill relied on regulation-writing and enforcement capacity at OSHA, so its real-world benefit would depend on the Labor Department writing the rules well and funding the new office, training, and toll-free line [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are substantial for workers in an industry with high fatality and injury rates: site-specific safety plans, inspection rights, and a stop-work mechanism address deaths and serious injuries directly. The costs are real but ordinary for safety regulation — administrative planning and liability allocation on construction projects — and the bill included flexibility for the Secretary to modify requirements for lower-risk work and exemptions for homeowners' own residences and emergency work [S3]. On balance this was a conventional, well-structured workplace safety bill whose main weakness was political: it attracted no cosponsors and no committee action.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Dodd introduced the bill on October 7, 1997, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S5, S1].
No further action was ever taken: the bill received no cosponsors, no hearing, no committee markup, and no floor vote in either chamber [S4, S5].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction owners and contractors are better off because the bill died: they avoided the cost of mandatory project safety plans, a new layer of citation liability for project constructors, and the risk of losing federal bids over poor safety records. Workers in a high-fatality industry did not get the protections.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 7, 1997 and delivered introductory remarks; it was his only recorded action on the measure.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator besides the sponsor signed on, so the record shows no partisan pattern — the bill simply never moved.

industries.note: The bill would have required designated project constructors, written safety plans, worksite inspections, and citation liability on every project, adding compliance costs. Those costs correspond to protections workers in one of the most dangerous industries lack, so the industry's cost is the public's gain.

Owners of projects with multiple prime contractors would default to being the project constructor and bear responsibility for the site safety plan. They would pay for a coordination role they did not previously hold.

The bill directed the Labor Department to recommend making bidders' safety records a criterion in federal construction contract awards, which would reward compliant contractors over competitors with poor records.
